name: Brahma Sirakandeeswarar Temple, Thirukandiyur
deity: Shiva as Brahma Sirakandeeswarar (Veerattaneswarar), with the goddess Mangalanayaki
period: Fifth shrine of the Saptha Sthanam and one of the Ashta Veerattanams; sung in the Tevaram (7th century), with Chola inscriptions from the 10th century
dynasty: Chola, with later Nayak and Maratha patronage
summary: At Thirukandiyur, Shiva is the Veerattaneswarar who struck off Brahma's fifth head to humble his pride: one of the eight Ashta Veerattanams, and the fifth temple of the Saptha Sthanam procession.

sections.history: Thirukandiyur lies on the road between Thanjavur and Thiruvaiyaru, a few kilometres south of Thiruvaiyaru, and it is home to two temples bound by one story: this Shiva shrine and, a short walk away, the Vishnu temple of Hara Saba Vimochana Perumal, a Divya Desam. Appar and Sambandar sang of the lord here, so the Shiva temple is a Paadal Petra Sthalam. An inscription of the Chola king Uttama Chola on the north wall of the central shrine shows that the temple was already receiving royal gifts in the tenth century, and later Chola, Thanjavur Nayak and Maratha rulers added endowments of their own.
sections.architecture: The temple is a Chola stone shrine enclosed by later walls and mandapams, with the sanctum of Brahma Sirakandeeswarar at its heart and a separate shrine for the goddess Mangalanayaki. Unusually for a Shiva temple, images of Brahma and Saraswati stand within the complex, outside the main sanctum; tradition says they were brought here when an older Brahma temple nearby fell into ruin. Brahma is seated with palms joined in prayer, holding a flower and a rudraksha rosary, as though still seeking pardon.
sections.legends: The sthala purana tells that Brahma, proud of his five heads, was once mistaken for Shiva and accepted an honour that was not his. To humble that pride, Shiva struck off his fifth head, a deed counted among the eight heroic acts remembered at the Ashta Veerattanams, and it gives the lord his name: Brahma Sirakandeeswarar, the lord who severed Brahma's head. The skull clung to Shiva's hand until it fell away at Thirukandiyur, and the nearby Vishnu temple tells the same story from its own side.
sections.festivals: In the Saptha Sthanam festival of Chithirai (April–May), Thirukandiyur is the fifth temple on the route, after Thiruvedhikudi, and its deities join the procession in their own glass palanquin. Tradition holds that the village provided ornaments for Nandi's wedding. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are kept through the year. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Thirukandiyur rewards a visit to both its temples. Come first to Brahma Sirakandeeswarar, pause before the rare images of Brahma and Saraswati, and then walk the few hundred metres to the Vishnu temple, where the story of the severed head finds its ending. Pilgrims on the round of the eight Veerattanams come here too, and because it stands on the main road it is the easiest of the seven Saptha Sthanam temples to reach.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but strictly prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Thirukandiyur is on the Thanjavur–Thiruvaiyaru road, about 3 km south of Thiruvaiyaru and roughly 10 km from Thanjavur, and town buses between the two stop here. Thanjavur is the nearest major railway station, and Tiruchirappalli International Airport, around 60 km away, is the nearest airport. The Hara Saba Vimochana Perumal temple is a short walk away.
